ATP, adenosine triphosphate, is the primary energy currency of cells. It's a small molecule consisting of adenosine, which is a nucleobase plus a five-carbon sugar, bonded to three phosphate groups. The high-energy bonds between these phosphate groups store chemical energy. When ATP releases a phosphate group, becoming ADP or AMP, that energy is released and used to drive cellular processes: muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, DNA replication, and countless other reactions. The continuous synthesis and breakdown of ATP couples energy-releasing reactions to energy-requiring reactions.

ATP consists of adenosine—the nucleobase adenine plus ribose sugar—bonded to a chain of three phosphate groups. The bonds between phosphate groups, especially the terminal bond between the second and third phosphates, are high-energy bonds. Their hydrolysis releases approximately thirty point five kilojoules per mole under standard conditions, though actual cellular conditions make this about fifty kilojoules per mole. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP plus inorganic phosphate is highly exergonic, meaning it releases energy. This energy is captured by enzymes and used to drive otherwise unfavorable reactions.

Let me explain ATP synthesis. Oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria works like this: the electron transport chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. ATP synthase harnesses this gradient to phosphorylate ADP plus phosphate into ATP. A single NADH oxidized through the electron transport chain yields approximately two and a half ATP. A single FADH two yields approximately one and a half ATP.

The complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yields roughly thirty to thirty-two ATP under optimal conditions, which is far more efficient than anaerobic fermentation, which yields only two ATP per glucose. Photophosphorylation in chloroplasts uses light energy directly to pump protons and drive ATP synthesis via the same ATP synthase mechanism. Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, where ATP is produced directly when a phosphate group is transferred from a high-energy intermediate to ADP.

ATP is consumed for many cellular purposes. Active transport uses ATP; pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase use ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient. Protein synthesis requires ATP; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use ATP to charge transfer RNAs, and the ribosome uses ATP or GTP to move along messenger RNA. Muscle contraction uses ATP; myosin heads use ATP to perform the power stroke, pulling actin filaments. DNA replication and repair use ATP; DNA polymerases and helicases use ATP and deoxynucleotide triphosphates. And biosynthesis, building new molecules like proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, requires ATP.

A typical human uses their body weight in ATP each day, yet contains only about point two moles of ATP at any moment. ATP must be recycled rapidly. ATP interconverts with ADP and AMP. The ratio of ATP to ADP and AMP reflects cellular energy status. AMP-activated protein kinase senses low energy, indicated by a high AMP to ATP ratio, and activates catabolic pathways while inhibiting anabolic pathways, balancing cellular energy. When ATP levels are high, feedback inhibition dampens glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and other catabolic pathways, preventing overproduction of ATP.

ATP, like other nucleotides, is built from the nucleobase adenine, the sugar ribose, and the phosphate groups. Its synthesis occurs via de novo and salvage pathways. ATP is also the source of nucleotides for RNA synthesis. The RNA polymerase uses ATP and GTP, CTP, and UTP as substrates. ATP synthesis and breakdown are tightly coupled to maintain cellular energy homeostasis.

ATP is often called the energy currency of life, and the metaphor is apt. Just as money enables exchange of goods and services in an economy, ATP enables the coupling of energy-releasing reactions to energy-requiring processes. The discovery of ATP and its role in energy metabolism was revolutionary. It explained how cells extract useful work from chemical reactions and unified biochemistry around a single molecule. The structure of ATP synthase—a rotary molecular motor driven by a proton gradient—is among the most elegant and exquisite discoveries in molecular biology.
